case.text: 2011-04-16 TRES, phase=9.16, Teff=6000, log(g)=3.5, Vrot=16, Vrad=-25.403, ccfPeak=0.906 1474C-SQ20110424.ps The light curve for this target looks strange. It appears as though the depth is getting shallower over time, and if my eyes are following each successive transit correctly (see *'s vs +'s), the time of mid-transit is shifting. It seems like there are some dynamics here and/or these are stellar eclipses. With a modeled companion radius of 1.75 R_J, it wouldn't surprise me to find that this is a false positive. Let's get another exposure to look for velocity variation. 2011-04-16 TRES, phase=9.16, Teff=6000, log(g)=3.5, Vrot=16, Vrad=-25.403, ccfPeak=0.906 2011-05-21 TRES, phase=9.66, Teff=6250, log(g)=4.0, Vrot=16, Vrad=-24.887, ccfPeak=0.935 1474C-SQ20110526.ps The velocity variation of 600 m/s is probably within the errors given that the spectra are from 2 different instruments. However, given the suspicious light curve ( here ), I wouldn't be surprised if the variation is due in part to an unseen companion or even the transiting object itself. This deserves more attention, but probably not more velocities right now. Those should be requested if there is evidence that they will be helpful. WIYN speckle imaging was taken of K01474 on 2011-06-15. The 2.8x2.8 arcsec FOV was centered on the target star. No secondary sources were detected. See separate plots/tables for the limiting magnitude of the field as a function of distance from the target star. The light from such a neighboring star, whether background or gravitationally bound to KOI-87, would fall in the slit of the Keck spectrometer causing its spectrum to contaminate that of the main star, KOI-87. Here is a description of what I did, written so that it may be useful as text in the ApJ paper on KOI-87 (with "we" substituted for "I"). To detect any companion star, I computed the cross-correlation function for a large wavelength region of the Keck-HIRES echelle spectrum, from 3600 - 6200 Angstroms. This region has few telluric lines, leaving the cross correlation dominated by stellar lines for FGKM stars. For the template I used a spectrum of Ganymede as a solar proxy. The cross-correlation function is very smooth, at the 1\\% level, from such a large wavelength range, and it nicely captures the shape of the thousands of absorption lines within that wavelength region. I then cross-correlated a library spectrum (from our vast collection of 2000 Keck spectra of FGKM star) of similar type, in this case HD 90156 (G5 V, Teff=5520 K). The goal is to compute the overall shape of the cross-correlation function from such stars, enabling a comparison of the CCF from KOI-87 to the CCF obtained with this comparison, library star. Indeed, the two cross-correlation functions came out with very similar shapes within 2\\% of the peak of the CCF. To detect the presence of any companion in KOI-87, I took the difference between the CCF(KOI-87) and CCF(HD 90156) to look for differences. Again, the differences were only typically 1-2\\% of the peak of the CCF, i.e. the two CCFs have nearly the same shape, as desired. I then injected a second spectrum of a G star into the spectrum of the KOI-87. This "fake" secondary spectrum can be adjusted to have any relative radial velocity and any relative intensity. This flexibility is similar to what BLENDER senses in its multi-dimensional parameter space. One may then simply compare the difference in CCFs, CCF(program star) - CCF(comparison), computed with and without the "fake" secondary spectrum. The fake secondary spectrum causes a "bump" in the CCF that departs from the CCF of the comparison star. Thus the difference between the two CCFs increases with increasing intensity of the fake secondary star. One may simply increase the relative intensity of the fake secondary star until the CCF of the this fake binary system departs significantly from the CCF of the library comparison star. For trails in which the difference in CCF caused by the secondary star becomes larger than the systematic noise of the CCF, the secondary star is detectable. Attached is a representative plot (.eps and .png) of CCF(KOI-87) - CCF(HD 90156) both as observed (dots) and also with a fake companion injected (solid line) in the spectrum of KOI-87. Thanks, Geoff [Observing notes 1 of 2] I have analyzed carefully the Keck spectrum we have of KOI-87 with the goal of detecting, or placing limits on, the spectrum from any additional neighboring star located within 0.5 arcsec. The light from such a neighboring star, whether background or gravitationally bound to KOI-87, would fall in the slit of the Keck spectrometer causing its spectrum to contaminate that of the main star, KOI-87. Here is a description of what I did, written so that it may be useful as text in the ApJ paper on KOI-87 (with "we" substituted for "I"). To detect any companion star, I computed the cross-correlation function for a large wavelength region of the Keck-HIRES echelle spectrum, from 3600 - 6200 Angstroms. This region has few telluric lines, leaving the cross correlation dominated by stellar lines for FGKM stars. For the template I used a spectrum of Ganymede as a solar proxy. The cross-correlation function is very smooth, at the 1\\% level, from such a large wavelength range, and it nicely captures the shape of the thousands of absorption lines within that wavelength region. I then cross-correlated a library spectrum (from our vast collection of 2000 Keck spectra of FGKM star) of similar type, in this case HD 90156 (G5 V, Teff=5520 K). The goal is to compute the overall shape of the cross-correlation function from such stars, enabling a comparison of the CCF from KOI-87 to the CCF obtained with this comparison, library star. Indeed, the two cross-correlation functions came out with very similar shapes within 2\\% of the peak of the CCF. To detect the presence of any companion in KOI-87, I took the difference between the CCF(KOI-87) and CCF(HD 90156) to look for differences. Again, the differences were only typically 1-2\\% of the peak of the CCF, i.e. the two CCFs have nearly the same shape, as desired. I then injected a second spectrum of a G star into the spectrum of the KOI-87. This "fake" secondary spectrum can be adjusted to have any relative radial velocity and any relative intensity. This flexibility is similar to what BLENDER senses in its multi-dimensional parameter space. One may then simply compare the difference in CCFs, CCF(program star) - CCF(comparison), computed with and without the "fake" secondary spectrum. The fake secondary spectrum causes a "bump" in the CCF that departs from the CCF of the comparison star. Thus the difference between the two CCFs increases with increasing intensity of the fake secondary star. One may simply increase the relative intensity of the fake secondary star until the CCF of the this fake binary system departs significantly from the CCF of the library comparison star. For trails in which the difference in CCF caused by the secondary star becomes larger than the systematic noise of the CCF, the secondary star is detectable. Attached is a representative plot (.eps and .png) of CCF(KOI-87) - CCF(HD 90156) both as observed (dots) and also with a fake companion injected (solid line) in the spectrum of KOI-87. For the case shown, the companion star has an intensity 0.025 of the primary star (i.e. 4 mag fainter), and it is separated by 30 km/s (typically of either a background star or bound companion at 1 AU).
